Audio that speaks to you wherever you are.
Listening Library presents Magic Treehouse Book Number One.
Dinosaurs Before Dark by Mary Pope Osborne.
Read for you by the author.
“A real monster in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.”
said Annie, She ran up the road, Oh, brother.
This is what he got for spending time with his sevenyear-old sister, Annie loved pretend stuff.
But Jack was eight and a half.
Annie raced alone into the woods.
The sun was about to set.
Jack left the road and headed into the woods.
The trees were lit with a golden late-afternoon light.
Standing under a tall oak tree.
She was pointing at a rope ladder.
The longest rope ladder Jack had ever seen.
The ladder went all the way up to the top of the tree.
There—at the top—was a tree house.
It was tucked between two branches.
“That must be the highest tree house in the world,” said Annie.
But I’m going up,” said Annie.
We don’t know who it belongs to," said Jack.
“Just for a teeny minute,” said Annie.
Annie disappeared inside the tree house.
He was about to call again when Annie poked her head out of the tree house window.
He pushed his glasses into place.
He gripped the sides of the rope ladder, and up he went.
Jack crawled through a hole in the tree house floor.
The tree house m filled with books.
Very old books with dusty covers.
New books with shiny, bright covers.
You can see far, far away,” said Annie.
She was peering out the tree house window.
Jack looked out the window with her, Down below were the tops of the other trees.
In the distance he saw the Frog Creek library.
The elementary school, The park, Annie pointed in the other direction.
There was their white wooden house with the green porch.
Next door was their neighbor’s black dog, Henry.
“We’re not supposed to be up here.”
He glanced around the tree house again.
“I wonder who owns all these books,” he said.
He noticed bookmarks were sticking out of many of them.
She held up a book with a castle on the cover.
“Here’s a book about Pennsylvania,” said Jack, He turned to the page with the bookmark.
“Hey, there’s a picture of Frog Creek in here,” said Jack.
“Oh, here’s a book for you,” said Annie.
She held up a book about dinosaurs.
A blue silk bookmark was sticking out of it.
Jack set down his backpack and grabbed the book from her.
“You look at that one, and I’ll look at the one about castles,” said Annie.
“We don’t know who these books belong But even as he said this, Jack opened the dinosaur book to where the bookmark was, He couldn’t help himself.
He turned to a picture of an ancient flying reptile.
He touched the huge bat-like wings.
“I wish I could see a Pteranodon for real.”
Jack studied the picture of the odd-looking creature soaring through the sky.
She pointed to the tree house window.
A giant creature was gliding above the treetops!
He had a long, weird crest on the back of his head.
It was a real live Pteranodon!
The creature curved through the sky.
He was coining straight toward the tree house.
He looked like a glider plane!
Jack nearly fell out the window trying to see it.
The tree house started to spin.
She pulled him back from the window.
The tree house was still high up in an oak tree.
But it wasn’t the same oak tree.
He looked down at the picture in the book.
He looked back out the window.
The world outside and the world in the picture—they were exactly the same.
The Pteranodon was soaring through the sky.
The ground was covered with ferns and tall grass.
The Pteranodon glided down to the base of their tree.
The creature coasted to a stop.
He looked at her, “I don’t know,” said Jack.
“I was looking at the picture in the book-” “And you said, 'Wow, I wish I could see a Pteranodon for real,’ ” said Annie.
In the Frog Creek woods,” said Jack.
And then the wind got loud.
And the tree house started spinning,” said Annie.
Annie looked out the window again.
“He’s very real,” Jack looked out the window with her.
The Pteranodon was standing at the base of the oak tree.
His giant wings were spread out on either side of him.
Annie called again to the creature.
The Pteranodon looked up at them.
“But maybe the book can tell us.”
Jack looked down at the book.
He read the words under the picture: This flying reptile lived in the Cretaceous period.
They couldn’t have landed in a time 65 million years ago.
Let’s go down and talk to him.”
Annie started down the rope ladder.
She stepped boldly up to the ancient creature.
Jack gasped as Annie held out her hand.
She was always trying to make friends with animals.
But this was going too far.
“Don’t get too close to him, Annie!”
Jack shouted, But Annie touched the Pteranodon’s crest, She stroked his neck.
What in the world was she saying?
It would be good to examine the creature.
Jack started down the rope ladder.
When he got to the ground, Jack was only a few feet away from the creature.
His eyes were bright and alert.
He brushed his hand down the creature’s neck.
A thin layer of fuzz covered the Pteranodon’s skin.
Jack reached into his backpack and pulled out a pencil and a notebook.
He wrote: FUZZY SKIN “What are you doing?”
“We’re probably the first people in the whole world to ever see a real live Pteranodon.”
Jack looked at the Pteranodon again.
The creature had a bony crest on top of his head.
The crest was longer than Jack’s arm.
“I wonder how smart he is,” Jack said, “Very smart,” said Annie.
“His brain’s probably no bigger than a bean.”
I can feel it,” said Annie.
Jack wrote in his notebook; SMALL BRAIN?
Jack looked at the creature again, “Maybe he’s a mutant,” he said.
Annie leaned close to the Pteranodon.
“Do you know where we are, Henry?”
The creature fixed his eyes on Annie.
His long jaws were opening and closing.
Like a giant pair of scissors.
“Are you trying to talk to me, Henry?”
Jack wrote in his notebook: MOUTH LIKE SCISSORS?
“Did we come to a time long ago, Henry?”
“Is this a place from long ago?”
Annie was pointing toward the hill.
On top stood a huge dinosaur!
He threw his notebook into his pack.
He pushed Annie toward the rope ladder.
He gave Annie a big push.
But she started up the ladder.
They tumbled into the tree house.
They were panting as they looked out the window at the dinosaur.
He was standing on the hilltop.
“We are in a time long ago!”
The dinosaur looked like a huge rhinoceros.
Only he had three horns instead of one.
Two long ones above his eyes and one on his nose.
He had a big shield-like thing behind his head.
He pointed to a picture of a Triceratops.
He read the caption; The Triceratops lived in the late Cretaceous period, This plant-eating dinosaur weighed over 12,000 pounds.
Jack slammed the book shut, “Just plants.
“Don’t you want to take notes about him?”
asked Annie, “We’re probably the first people in the whole world to ever see a real live Triceratops.”
He shoved the dinosaur book into his pack.
He slung it over his shoulder and started down the ladder.
On the way down, Jack stopped.
He called up to Annie, “Just promise you won’t pet him.”
When they stepped off the ladder, the Pteranodon gave them a kind look.
Annie blew a kiss at him.
“Be back soon, Henry,” she said cheerfully.
And he led the way through the ferns.
When he reached the bottom of the hill, he kneeled behind a fat bush.
Annie knelt beside him and started to speak.
Jack put his finger to his lips.
Jack peeked out at the Triceratops.
He was eating the flowers off a magnolia tree.
Jack slipped his notebook out of his pack, He wrote; EATS FLOWERS Annie nudged him.
He wrote: EATS SLOWLY Annie nudged him hard.
She walked her fingers through the air.
In full view of the Triceratops!
The big dinosaur had spotted Annie.
He gazed down at her from the hilltop.
Half of a magnolia flower was sticking out of his mouth.
Jack shouted at her, “He looks nice, Jack.”
Watch out for his horns, Annie!"
But the Triceratops just gazed calmly down at Annie.
Then he turned and loped away.
Down the side of the hill.
But he wrote in his notebook: NICE “Come on.
Let’s look around some more,” said Annie.
As Jack started after Annie, he saw something glittering in the tall grass.
He reached out and picked it up.
A letter was engraved on the medallion, A fancy M.
Someone came here before us,” Jack said softly.
Annie had gone up to the hilltop.
She was busy picking a flower from the magnolia tree.
But Annie wasn’t paying attention to Jack, She was staring at something on the other side of the hill.
Clutching her magnolia flower, she took off down the hill.
“I’m going to kill her,” Jack muttered.
He stuffed the gold medallion into his jeans pocket.
Jack heard another sound as well.
Jack grabbed his backpack and raced up the hill.
When he got to the top, he gasped.
The valley below was filled with nests.
Big nests made out of mud.
And the nests were filled with tiny dinosaurs!
Annie was crouching next to one of the nests, And standing over her was a gigantic duck-billed dinosaur!
He stepped slowly down the hill toward Annie.
The huge dinosaur was towering above Annie.
He didn’t want to get too close.
Clutching her flower, Annie crawled toward Jack.
Jack inched farther down the hill.
Until he was just an arm’s distance from Annie.
He reached out—and grabbed her hand, He pulled Annie toward him.
He crouched next to her, “Bow your head.
I read that’s what you do if a mean dog comes at you.”
Jack and Annie both bowed their heads.
“I don’t think she’s mad anymore,” he said.
“Thanks, Jack, for saving me,” said Annie.
"You have to use your brain,” said Jack.
“You can’t just go running to a nest of babies.
Annie held out her magnolia flower to the dinosaur.
“I’m sorry I made you worry about your babies,” she said.
The dinosaur moved closer to Annie.
She grabbed the flower from her.
The dinosaur let out a sad tuba sound.
“But there are more flowers up there," Annie said.
She pointed to the top of the hill.
Some were crawling out of their nests.
Jack took out the dinosaur book.
He flipped through the pages, He found a picture of some duck-billed dinosaurs.
He read the caption: The Anatosauruses lived in colonies.
While a few mothers babysat the nests, others hunted for food.
So there must be more mothers close by.
Annie was at the top of the hill.
Feeding magnolia flowers to the giant Anatosaurus!
But suddenly the Anatosaurus made her terrible tuba sound.
Annie crouched down and started to chew.
The dinosaur barged down the hill.
Jack put the book down on top of his pack.
“I wonder why she ran away,” said Annie.
What he saw in the distance almost made him throw up.
An enormous ugly monster was coming across the plain.
He was walking on two big legs.
And swinging a long, thick tail.
And his jaws were wide open.
Even from far away Jack could see his long, gleaming teeth.
They dashed down the hill together.
Through the tall grass, through the ferns, past the Pteranodon, and right to the rope ladder, They scrambled up, Seconds later they tumbled into the tree house.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
He looked through the window with her.
But then the monster stopped and turned around.
The two of them hunched down.
After a long moment, they raised their heads.
“We have to get out of here,” said Jack.
“You made a wish before,” said Annie.
“I wish we could go back to Frog Creek,” said Jack.
You were looking at a picture in the dinosaur book.
I left the book and my pack on the hill.
Plus my notebook’s in my pack.
Jack hurried down the rope ladder.
He raced past the Pteranodon, through the ferns, through the tall grass, and up the hill, He looked down.
There was his pack, lying on the ground.
On top of it was the dinosaur book, But now the valley below was filled with Anatosauruses.
All standing guard around the nests.
Did fear of the Tyrannosaurus send them home?
All the Anatosauruses were bellowing at him.
He raced up to the hilltop.
And he was standing between Jack and the tree house!
Jack jumped behind the magnolia tree.
His heart was beating so fast he could hardly think.
He peeked out at the giant monster, The horriblelooking creature was opening and closing his huge jaws.
His teeth were as big as steak knives, Don’t panic.
Jack peered down at the valley.
Good, The duck-billed dinosaurs were sticking close to their nests.
Jack looked back at the pteranosaurus.
Good, The monster still didn’t seem to know he was there, Don’t panic.
Maybe there’s information in the book.
He read: Tyrannosaurus rex was the largest meat-eating land animal of all time.
If it were alive today, it would eat a human in one bite.
The book was no help at all.
He couldn’t hide on the other side of the hill.
He couldn’t run to the tree house.
Wait for the monster to leave.
The Tyrannosaurus had wandered closer to the hill.
Annie was coming down the rope ladder!
Jack watched Annie hop off the ladder.
She went straight to the Pteranodon.
She pointed at Jack, at the sky, at the tree house.
The Tyrannosaurus rex was looking in his direction.
The Tyrannosaurus rex was coming toward the hill.
Just then a giant shadow covered Jack.
The giant creature sailed down toward the top of the hill.
He was coming straight for Jack.
The Pteranodon coasted down to the ground.
He stared at Jack with his bright, alert eyes.
What was Jack supposed to do?
He was starting up the hill.
His giant teeth were flashing in the sunlight.
Jack put his book in his pack.
Then he eased down onto the Pteranodon’s back.
He spread out his wings-and lifted off the ground!
The Pteranodon steadied himself, then rose into the sky.
The Tyrannosaurus was chomping the air and staring up at him.
Over all the nests filled with babies.
Over all the giant duck-billed dinosaurs.
Then the Pteranodon soared out over the plain-over the Triceratops who was grazing in the high grass.
The wind was rushing through his hair.
The air smelled sweet and fresh.
He was riding on the back of an ancient flying reptile!
The Pteranodon sailed over the stream, over the ferns and bushes.
Then he carried Jack down to the base of the oak tree.
When they came to a stop, Jack slid off the creature’s back.
Then the Pteranodon took off again and glided into the sky.
Annie shouted from the tree house.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
He kept staring up at the Pteranodon.
“Thanks for saving my life,” he said.
The Tyrannosaurus was heading straight toward him!
He grabbed the sides and started up.
Jack scrambled into the tree house.
Suddenly something slammed against the oak tree.
The tree house shook like a leaf.
Jack and Annie tumbled into the books.
The one with the picture of Frog Creek!”
He had to find that book about Pennsylvania.
He grabbed it and tore through it, looking for the photograph of the Frog Creek woods.
"I wish we could go home," he shouted.
The tree house started to spin.
He held on tightly to Annie.
He was still pointing at the picture of the Frog Creek woods.
He peeked out the tree house window.
Outside he saw the exact same view.
The woods were lit with a golden late-afternoon light.
The sun was about to set.
No time had passed since they’d left “Ja-ack!
a voice called from the distance.
Jack saw their mother far away.
She was standing in front of their house.
Annie stuck her head out the window and shouted, "Coming!"
“We took a trip in a magic tree house,” said Annie simply.
“But it’s the same time as when we left,” said Jack.
“And how did it take us so far away?”
“You just looked at a book and said you wished we could go there,” said Annie.
“And the magic tree house took us there.”
“And who built this magic tree house?
Who put all these books here?”
"A magic person, I guess," said Annie.
He reached into his pocket and pulled out the gold medallion.
Look, there’s a letter M on it.”
“You think M stands for magic person?”
“I just know someone went to that place before us.”
Annie poked her head out the window.
Jack put the gold medallion back in his pocket.
He pulled the dinosaur book out of his pack And put it back with all the other books, Then he and Annie took one last look around the tree house.
Jack slung his backpack over his shoulder.
Seconds later they hopped onto the ground and started walking out of the woods.
“No one’s going to believe our story,” said Jack.
"So let's not tell anyone," said Annie.
“He’ll say it was a dream,” said Annie.
“My teacher won’t believe it," said Jack.
“We better not tell anyone,” said Jack.
“I think I’m starting to not believe it myself,” he said.
They left the woods and started up the road toward their house.
As they walked past all the houses on their street, the trip to dinosaur time did seem more and more like a dream.
Only this world and this time seemed real.
He felt the engraving of the letter M.
He couldn’t explain what had happened today.
But he knew for sure that their trip in the magic tree house had been real.
“Tomorrow," Jack said softly, “we’ll go back to the woods.”
“And we’ll climb up to the tree house," said Jack.
“And we’ll see what happens next,” said Jack, “Of course,” said Annie.
And they took off together, running for home.
